I recently read Intellectuals and Society by Thomas Sowell. It's an analysis of the allure of hubris among elites and how that effect drives policy changes. The thesis, you might say, is that highly educated individuals flock to certain views because they gain a sense that because they are more educated, they are better qualified to set policy in all areas and to prefer policies which take decisions away from the people at large and place them in the hands of the elites (who again, are presumed better able to decide).

Sowell argues in the book that this is a poor approach for two primary reasons: first, a master of one subject doesn't necessarily know anything about others: a physician may be extremely well educated, yet know nothing about economics, international relations or even governance in general. Second, in many ways collective knowledge is greater than individual knowledge can possible hope to be; even the most brilliant person ever to live cannot possibly know the details and needs of the lives of 300 million people better than each of those people know themselves.

It's a very well researched and analyzed book; I'd recommend it.
